channel.title: Niansia · Blog
channel.description: Monthly updates, notes on the papers I read and what I make of them, and answers to your questions.

item.title: RINE: do intermediate layers know “fake” better than the last one?
item.description: RINE detects generated images from CLIP's intermediate layers, and my own experiments largely agree. Under real-world corruptions, though, the most useful layers change, and the breadth of augmentation matters more than which layer the features come from.

item.title: September 2026: new projects and an exam gallery, CVPR prep begins
item.description: This month Taiwan Exam, its exam gallery, the in-browser LumiGrid and Adversarial Lab went live, and the site moved to niansia.com. Next up is the CVPR 2027 submission in mid-November.

item.title: Reroute: can dropped visual tokens come back later?
item.description: Reroute turns "delete the low-scoring visual tokens" into "defer them, and let them come back", with no training, and the harder the compression, the more it recovers. We are studying how to recover and re-locate what a long video loses in compression, and this paper attacks the smallest version of that problem.

item.title: SwarmWorld: agents cooperate without talking — is watching their messages enough?
item.description: Identical LLM agents dropped into a world that keeps their traces divide the work among themselves with no assigned roles, and mostly learn each other's technology by walking past it. The announcement was dramatic, the paper is far more measured; what I care about most is the security angle — watching only what agents say to each other misses a lot of coordination.

item.title: Act2See: the model learns to look back — what if you don't have eight A100s?
item.description: Act2See lets a video model stop mid-reasoning to fetch a frame from the video, or draw a hypothetical one, and it beats its base model on all five benchmarks. It was trained on eight A100s, though, and I kept asking myself how the same idea would work on a single home GPU.

item.title: VTC-R1: printing the reasoning as images and using them as scratch paper
item.description: VTC-R1 renders each finished stretch of reasoning into images, and in the next round the model continues from that "scratch paper" alone. Tokens drop 3.4×, speed goes up 1.2–6.6×, and accuracy is mostly higher. It is a lovely idea, but every task is text-only math, nobody measures whether the scratch paper is read back correctly, and video reasoning, where visual tokens are already overflowing, is a different matter.

item.title: VisionPulse: at every step of the reasoning, the model needs to see something different
item.description: VisionPulse finds that a model's reliance on the image changes from one reasoning step to the next, so at each step it keeps only the visual tokens needed right then. With 5% kept, accuracy barely moves and the reasoning gets shorter. I love the observation; but it saves compute rather than memory, the experiments are all on images, and the double explosion of long video plus long reasoning is still untouched.

item.title: V-Skip: when you shorten the reasoning, don't cut out what the model saw
item.description: Move a text-only chain-of-thought compressor onto a vision-language model and it deletes the words that only the image could supply. The reasoning still reads smoothly, but it has come loose from the picture, and hallucinations follow. The paper calls this Visual Amnesia and it names a real problem; I have reservations about its explanation of the cause and about a few of its numbers.
